name: Fortran (gfortran) in niklas-heer/speed-comparison: Leibniz pi series
baseline: C (gcc 15.2.0, -O3 -flto -march=native with -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math) and the clang / C++ builds of the same Leibniz loop in the same suite
workload: Single-threaded Leibniz series for pi, 1,000,000,000 terms per run, three recorded runs per target (TimesPerRun in the raw JSON), median wall time.
claimed_speedup: Published snapshot 2026-09-05T193245, combined_results.csv medians in ms: Fortran 90 (gfortran 14.3.0) 141.67 vs C (gcc 15.2.0) 157.9, about 1.11x (derived from page data); vs C++ (g++) 158.78, about 1.12x (derived); vs C (clang 21.1.2) 146.07, about 1.03x (derived); vs C++ (clang++) 143.32, about 1.01x (derived). Min-max ranges: Fortran 141.04-144.35 ms, C++ clang++ 142.74-144.96 ms, C (clang) 143.63-150.61 ms, C (gcc) 155.46-160.78 ms, so the lead over the clang builds is inside the sample range.
compiler_and_flags: Fortran: gfortran 14.3.0 `gfortran leibniz.f90 -o leibniz -Ofast -flto -ffast-math -march=native -mtune=native`. C: gcc 15.2.0 `gcc -O3 -s -flto -march=native -mtune=native -fomit-frame-pointer -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math -o leibniz leibniz.c -lm`. C++ clang++ 21.1.2 and C clang 21.1.2 use the same flag set (from docs/history/2026-09-05T193245/raw/*.json).
hardware: AMD EPYC-Genoa Processor, 4 threads, shared x86-64 VM (runner homelab-argo), kernel 6.18.38-talos
tradeoffs: The suite compares single implementations of one arithmetic loop, not Fortran as a whole. The Fortran loop is written differently from the C loop: it is unrolled by hand to four terms per iteration (src/leibniz.f90), while C/C++ use a one-term loop with an `i & 1` sign trick written to allow vectorisation (src/leibniz.c).
caveats: Evidence would qualify as A (code, compiler versions, flags and CPU model are all public) but the source states no mechanism, so the tier is capped at C. The margin over the best C/C++ build (clang++ 143.32 ms) is about 1% and inside the three-sample ranges; the suite's own README warns that three samples cannot establish a winner for small differences. Flags are not matched: gfortran is built with -Ofast (includes -ffast-math and -freciprocal-math) while C sets only -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math, and the compiler versions differ (gfortran 14.3.0 vs gcc 15.2.0). The suite's accuracy column shows 9.440 correct digits for Fortran vs 9.499 for C and a 12-digit printout for Fortran, consistent with different arithmetic (not verified). Nim (142.43 ms) and Rust SIMD (141.31 ms) are also faster than gcc C in the same snapshot; Nim compiles through gcc, so that gap comes from source form, not language. Explicit-SIMD C++ (AVX2) is slower (290.67 ms). In the earlier snapshot docs/history/2025-12-14T070941 (gfortran 14.2.0) Fortran took 238.94 ms: about 1.06x faster than C (gcc) 253.23 ms (derived from page data) but slower than C++ (clang++) 223.89 ms and level with C (clang) 237.46 ms, so only the lead over gcc-built C is repeatable. The HEAD pipeline/languages.py pins different compiler versions than the snapshot; the snapshot's per-target JSON was used here.

name: V (clang backend) in LangArena: CLBG::Fannkuchredux
baseline: C in the same suite: C/Gcc `make prod` (gcc -O2 with hardening), the -O3 -march=native `Fast` builds, and the suite's other C and C++ build variants (Fast, Unsafe, PGO, mycc, cproc)
workload: CLBG fannkuch-redux (permutation flipping over a 32-int array), same algorithm in every language, runtime of the benchmark in seconds.
claimed_speedup: 2026-10-05 run, CLBG::Fannkuchredux runtime in s: V/Clang 0.875 vs C/Gcc 1.036, about 1.18x (derived from page data); C/Clang 1.174; C/Gcc/Fast (-O3 -march=native) 1.364, about 1.56x slower than V (derived); C/Clang/Fast 1.278; C++/Clang++ 1.128; C++/G++ 1.199. V/Clang/Perf (clang -O3 -march=native -flto) 0.912. The best gcc or clang C/C++ build was C/Gcc in all four monthly runs (1.020-1.047 s) and V/Clang was 0.862-0.879 s in each (results files 2026-08-14, 2026-09-03, 2026-09-18, 2026-10-05).
compiler_and_flags: V 0.5.1 `v -enable-globals -cc clang -prod` (clang 22.1.8). C baseline rows (c/Makefile): prod = gcc -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now (gcc 16 trunk r16-8246) or clang 22.1.8; Fast = -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe with LTO; Unsafe = -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer with full LTO.
tradeoffs: V transpiles to C and relies on the system C compiler; the V toolchain is young and less portable than gcc or clang. Benchmarks are written in the suite's safe, idiomatic style.
caveats: The C `prod` rows are -O2 with stack protector and frame pointers, not -O3, and the V row is not built with -march=native, so flags are not matched; however the -O3 Fast and -ffast-math Unsafe C/C++ builds are also slower on this test (1.137-1.364 s), so the optimisation level does not explain the gap. V emits C, so the gap is between V-generated C and the hand-written C in the suite, not a compiler-codegen advantage of a different language. Reading both sources: the C version copies each permutation with a runtime-length memcpy and swaps through pointer helpers; the V version copies with a plain loop and swaps inline. The suite states no mechanism, so the tier is capped at C. One benchmark only: V is slower than C elsewhere (Nbody 1.86 s vs 1.465 s). Gossamer (0.913 s) and Nim (0.918 s) also beat C here.

name: Nim (clang backend) in LangArena: CLBG::Fannkuchredux
baseline: C in the same suite: C/Gcc `make prod` (gcc -O2 with hardening), the -O3 -march=native `Fast` builds, and the suite's other C and C++ build variants (Fast, Unsafe, PGO, mycc, cproc)
workload: CLBG fannkuch-redux (permutation flipping over a 32-int array), same algorithm in every language, runtime of the benchmark in seconds.
claimed_speedup: 2026-10-05 run, CLBG::Fannkuchredux runtime in s: Nim/Clang 0.918 vs C/Gcc 1.036, about 1.13x (derived from page data); C/Clang 1.174; C/Gcc/Fast 1.364; C/Clang/Fast 1.278. Other Nim rows: Nim/Clang/ARC 0.934, Nim/NLVM 0.944. Nim/Clang was 0.918-0.933 s in all four monthly runs against 1.020-1.047 s for the best gcc or clang C/C++ build.
compiler_and_flags: Nim 2.2.12 `nim c --threads:on -d:release --cc:clang` (clang 22.1.8). C baseline rows (c/Makefile): prod = gcc -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now (gcc 16 trunk r16-8246) or clang 22.1.8; Fast = -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe with LTO; Unsafe = -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer with full LTO.
tradeoffs: Nim compiles to C and then to native code via the system C compiler, so the claim is about the C that Nim emits (garbage collection mode, bounds checks and overflow checks follow -d:release defaults).
caveats: Same limits as the other fannkuch-redux rows in this suite: C `prod` is -O2 with hardening and the Nim row is not built with -march=native, so flags are not matched, but the -O3 Fast and -ffast-math C/C++ builds are also slower on this test (1.137-1.364 s). Nim emits C, so the gap is Nim-generated C versus hand-written C, and the Nim source was not read here. The suite states no mechanism, so the tier is capped at C. One benchmark only: Nim is slower than C on Nbody (1.73 s vs 1.465 s) and Matmul (8.5 s vs 5.0 s single-thread).

name: Zig (ReleaseSafe) in LangArena: CLBG::Fannkuchredux
baseline: C in the same suite: C/Gcc `make prod` (gcc -O2 with hardening), the -O3 -march=native `Fast` builds, and the suite's other C and C++ build variants (Fast, Unsafe, PGO, mycc, cproc)
workload: CLBG fannkuch-redux (permutation flipping over a 32-int array), same algorithm in every language, runtime of the benchmark in seconds.
claimed_speedup: 2026-10-05 run, CLBG::Fannkuchredux runtime in s: Zig 0.977 vs C/Gcc 1.036, about 1.06x (derived from page data); C/Clang 1.174; C/Gcc/Fast 1.364; C/Clang/Fast 1.278. Zig stayed at 0.972-0.989 s in the four monthly runs (2026-08-14 to 2026-10-05) against 1.020-1.047 s for the best gcc or clang C/C++ build. Zig/Unchecked (ReleaseFast) is slower than the safe build at 1.024 s.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.17.0 `zig build build-zig` (build.zig: optimize = ReleaseSafe, runtime safety checks on). C baseline rows (c/Makefile): prod = gcc -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now (gcc 16 trunk r16-8246) or clang 22.1.8; Fast = -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe with LTO; Unsafe = -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer with full LTO.
tradeoffs: The default Zig row keeps bounds and overflow checks enabled and still beats the C builds, but the margin to the best C row is only about 6%.
caveats: Small margin on one benchmark, close to run-to-run variation (the unchecked ReleaseFast build is slower than the safe build, which points to code-layout noise). C `prod` is -O2 with hardening, so flags are not matched with the Zig ReleaseSafe build, but the -O3 Fast C/C++ builds are also slower on this test (1.198-1.364 s). The Zig loop is written differently from the C loop (`while i < j` with a decrementing j, versus the C precomputed k2 count) and Zig uses @memcpy; the suite states no mechanism, so the tier is capped at C. Zig is slower than C on Matmul and several other numeric rows in the same file.

name: Mojo in LangArena: CLBG::Nbody
baseline: C and C++ in the same suite at -O3: C/Gcc/Fast, C/Clang/Fast, C++/G++/Fast, C++/Clang++/Fast (-O3 -march=native with LTO), plus the -O2 `prod` rows and the -ffast-math `Unsafe` rows
workload: CLBG n-body (5 bodies, pairwise force update, Float64), same algorithm in every language, runtime of the benchmark in seconds.
claimed_speedup: 2026-10-05 run, CLBG::Nbody runtime in s: Mojo 1.1458 vs C/Gcc/Fast 1.221, about 1.07x (derived from page data); C/Clang/Fast 1.234; C++/G++/Fast 1.226; C++/Clang++/Fast 1.236; C/Gcc prod (-O2) 1.465. The -ffast-math Unsafe builds are on par or ahead: C++/Clang++/Unsafe 1.137, C/Clang/Unsafe 1.14, C++/G++/Unsafe 1.189, C/Gcc/Unsafe 1.193. In the 2026-09-03 and 2026-09-18 runs Mojo took 1.493 s, slower than the C -O3 rows, so the win appears only in the newest run (Mojo 1.1.0).
compiler_and_flags: Mojo 1.1.0 (8189361e) `pixi run mojo build -O3 main.mojo`. C baseline rows (c/Makefile): prod = gcc -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now (gcc 16 trunk r16-8246) or clang 22.1.8; Fast = -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe with LTO; Unsafe = -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer with full LTO.
tradeoffs: Young toolchain whose licence terms were not checked here; the same result file shows Mojo about 2x slower than C on Fannkuchredux (2.03 s vs 1.036 s) and about 4x slower on Matmul::Single (20.3 s vs 4.9 s), so this is a single favourable row.
caveats: Single run of the newest Mojo release; earlier monthly runs show no win (1.493 s). The Mojo runtime values carry nine decimal places while every other language has three, which suggests a different timing path (not verified). Not clearly better than C built with -O3 -ffast-math (1.137 s). Reading the sources, the Mojo code copies each planet into local values (value semantics) and writes it back, while the C code updates two bodies through pointers into one array that the compiler may have to treat as aliasing; the suite itself states no mechanism, so the tier is capped at C. Mojo licence terms were not checked; the repo licence listed is the suite's MIT.
found_via: GitHub: kostya/LangArena README (Mojo section) and results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js plus the 2026-09-03 and 2026-09-18 result files; mojo/nbody.mojo and c/src/nbody.c compared
